raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|turn|6540|turnbuckle}}</noinclude><poem>The charm of this enchanted ground,
And all its thousand ''turns'' disclose
Some fresher beauty varying round.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iii. 55 (song).}}}}

(''c'') A variation in the course of events; a change in the order, position, tendency, or aspect of things; hence, change in general; chance; happening; befalling.
{{smaller block|<poem>O ’Tis a Heav’nly and a happy ''turn'',
Of godly Parents to be timely born.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Fathers.}}
’Tis a happy ''Turn'' for us, when Kings are made Friends again. This was the end of this Embassy, and I hope it will last our days. {{right|''Lister'', Journey to Paris, p. 3.}}
<poem>Blame not the ''turns'' of fate, and chance of war.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', The Campaign.}}}}

(''d'') Turning-point; crisis; the point at which a change must come: as, the ''turn'' of the year; the ''turn'' of a fever.
{{smaller block|And yet the spring was breaking forth, as it always does in Devonshire when the ''turn'' of the days is even.
{{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Lorna Doone, vii.}}}}

(''e'') A twist, bias, or cast.
{{smaller block|It would, in fact, be almost impossible to give a tragic ''turn'' to any proceedings for contempt of Court.
{{right|''H. Hall'', Society in Elizabethan Age, x.}}}}

'''3.''' Form; shape; mold.
{{smaller block|I have sometimes wondered to see the Roman poets, in their descriptions of a beautiful man, so often mentioning the ''turn'' of his neck and arms, that in our modern dresses lie out of sight, and are covered under part of the clothing.
{{right|''Addison'', Ancient Medals, ii.}}}}

'''4.''' Tendency; bent; aptitude; disposition; humor: as, a person of a lively ''turn''.
{{smaller block|A man should always go with inclination to the ''turn'' of the company he is going into, or not pretend to be of the party. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 386.}}}}

{{smaller block|This Abd el cader no sooner was arrived at Masuah than, following the ''turn'' of his country for lying, he spread a report that a great man or prince whom he left at Jidda was coming speedily to Masuah.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, I. 292.}}}}
{{smaller block|I never had the least ''turn'' for dress — never any notion of fancy or elegance.
{{right|''Miss Burney'', Evelina, lxxxiii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Mrs. Bennet had no ''turn'' for economy.
{{right|''Jane Austen'', Pride and Prejudice, p. 261.}}}}
{{smaller block|But these things must have come to you with your mother’s blood. I never knew a Pyncheon that had any ''turn'' for them.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, v.}}}}

'''5.''' Particular form or character; mode; style.
{{smaller block|The Turk I mention’d . . . came after this happen’d to see me, who I found was so disagreeable to the Aga that he order’d him to leave the house, giving it this ''turn'', that he would not permit the people to come and teize me for presents.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, I. 119.}}}}
{{smaller block|The very ''turn'' of voice, the good pronunciation, and the polite and alluring manner which some teachers have attained will engage the attention.
{{right|''Watts'', Improvement of the Mind, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The conventional atmosphere of a drawing-room, in which the gravest problems were apt to be forgotten in the flash of an epigram or the ''turn'' of a bon mot.
{{right|''The Century'', XLI. 804.}}}}
{{smaller block|No man rallies with a better grace, and in more sprightly ''turns''.
{{right|''Swift'', Tale of a Tub, Ep. Ded.}}}}

'''6.''' In ''music'', a melodic embellishment or grace, consisting of a principal tone with two auxiliary tones lying respectively next above and below it in the diatonic series. {{smaller|It is indicated by the sign ~. When the sign is placed over the given note the upper auxiliary tone is sounded first; but when it is placed after}}
{{smaller block|the given note that note is sounded first. Chromatic alterations are indicated by accidentals over or under the sign. A turn occurring in two parts at once is called ''double'', and is indicated by the sign ≂. A turn in which the lower auxiliary tone is performed first is called ''inverted'' or a ''back-turn'', and is indicated by the sign 𝆗.}}
'''7.''' One round or return of rope, cord, or the like, when laid in a coil or skein.—'''8.''' A short walk, ride, or drive which includes a going and a returning; a promenade.
{{smaller block|You and I must walk a ''turn'' together.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., v. 1. 94.}}
He told me that his master came to town last night, and would be glad to take a ''turn'' with me in Grays-Inn walks.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 269.}}
Moore left his desk, and permitted himself the recreation of one or two ''turns'' through the room.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xxviii.}}}}
'''9.''' A spell, as of work; a job: as, he has not done a ''turn'' of work for several months.
{{smaller block|Not able . . . to do a hand’s ''turn'' for myself.
{{right|''Lever'', Davenport Dunn, v.}}}}
'''10.''' Opportunity or privilege enjoyed in alternation with another or with others; the time or occasion which comes in due rotation or order has to be got or to be done; recurring chance or opportunity.
{{smaller block|<poem>The nymph will have her ''turn'' to be
The tutor; and the pupil, he.</poem>
{{right|''Swift'', Cadenus and Vanessa.}}}}
{{smaller block|Even the few solitaries left on guard at Mr. Atkinson’s . . . condescend a little, as they drowsily bide or recall their ''turn'' chasing the ebbing Neptune on the ribbed sea-sand. {{right|''Dickens'', Uncommercial Traveller, xvi.}}}}
'''11.''' An act; deed; especially, an incidental or opportune act, deed, office, or service; act of kindness or of malice: as, a shrewd ''turn''.
{{smaller block|In requyting a good ''tourne'', shew not thy selfe negligent nor contrarye. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 106.}}}}
{{smaller block|For your kindness I owe you a good ''turn''.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 2. 62.}}}}
{{smaller block|One good ''turn'' requires another.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Little French Lawyer, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Chilon was wont to say, That it is commendable in men to forget bad ''turnes'' done, but to bee mindefull of courtesies receiued. {{right|''Heywood'', Hierarchy of Angels, p. 535.}}}}
'''12.''' A stratagem; a trick.
{{smaller block|Of all the ''tornes'' that he cowthe he schewed him but oon.
{{right|''Tale of Gamelyn'', l. 244.}}}}
'''13.''' Convenience; requirement; emergency; present need: as, to serve one’s ''turn''.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Pilia.'' Jew, I must have more gold.
''Bar.'' Why, want’st thou any of thy tale?
''Pilia.'' No, but three hundred will not serve his ''turn''.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe'', Jew of Malta, iv. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But for my daughter Katherine, this I know,
She is not for your ''turn''. ''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1. 63.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|And if the garden would not serve their ''turn'', then was the park the fittest place.
{{right|''Court and Times of Charles I.'', I. 33.}}}}

[[File:century v08 p0344 c1f1.png|center|175px]]

{{smaller block|The Bible is shut against them [hinderers of reformation] as certaine that neither Plato nor Aristotle is for their ''turnes.''
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}}
'''14.''' A nervous shock, such as is caused by alarm or sudden excitement. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|What a hard-hearted monster you must be, John, not to have said so at once, and saved me such a ''turn!''
{{right|''Dickens'', Cricket on the Hearth, ii.}}
Mrs. Tulliver gave a little scream as she saw her, and felt such a ''turn'' that she dropped the large gravy-spoon into the dish, with the most serious results to the tablecloth.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 7.}}}}
'''15†.''' An execution by hanging: from the former practice of making the criminal stand on a ladder, which was turned over at a signal, leaving him suspended.—'''16†.''' In ''law'', same as ''tourn.'' —'''17.''' ''pl.'' In ''med.'', monthly courses; menses.— '''18.''' In ''furriery'', a bundle of five dozen skins. —'''19.''' A load; a pack; as much as can be carried at one time by a man or an animal.
{{smaller block|Sometimes he would bring a ''turn'' of wood, sometimes a bag of meal or potatoes.
{{right|''J. C. Harris'', Harper’s Mag., LXXVI. 704.}}}}
'''20.''' In ''printing'', a type turned upside down and showing black in proof, as a temporary substitute for a letter that is missing; also, a letter wrongly placed so that the face is turned.
{{smaller block|He shows a curious printer’s blunder at the end of one page, where the whole of the last reference-line is put in upside down. . . . A ''turn'' of this magnitude could hardly have occurred if the letters had been set in the forme type by type.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIII. 693.}}}}
{{smaller|'''By turns.''' (''a'') One after another; alternately; in succession.}}
{{smaller block|Every one of the fiue went through the guard to fetch a childe each after other ''by turns.''
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', Works, I. 140.}}
''By turns'' to that, ''by turns'' to this a prey,
She knows what reason yields, and dreads what madness may.
{{right|''Crabbe'', Works, I. 51.}}
And love and prayer unite, or rule the hour ''by turns.''
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, i. 67.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') At intervals.}}
{{smaller block|Feel ''by turns'' the bitter change.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 598.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Dead turns.''' A dynamo-electric machine through which the current is kept constant is found to have an electromotive force nearly proportional to the angular velocity of the armature less a constant. This constant, expressed in turns per second or per minute, has been called the ''dead turns'' of the machine.—'''Direct turn,''' in ''music,'' an ordinary turn, as distinguished from an inverted turn.—'''Ill turn.''' (''a'') An unkind, injurious, or spiteful act. (''b'') A change for the worse, especially in a case of illness.—'''In turn,''' in due order of succession.—'''On the turn,''' at the turning-point; hence, changing; altering; on the point of or in process of reversal: as, the tide is now ''on the turn;'' our fortunes are ''on the turn.''}}
{{smaller block|And now by-gynneth thi gyle a-gayn ''on the turne,''
And my grace to growe ay wydder and wydder.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxi. 402.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Partial turn,''' in ''music,'' a turn in which the last tone is prolonged, so that the first three tones amount to a triple appoggiatura. In a slow tempo a turn on a long note is usually thus rendered.—'''Racking turns.''' See ''rack''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Round turn.''' See ''round''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Sheriff’s turn.''' See ''sheriff''<sup>1</sup>.—'''The turn of a hair.''' See ''hair''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To a turn,''' to a nicety; exactly; perfectly: as, the meat is done ''to a turn:'' from the practice of roasting meat on a revolving spit.}} minuteness of attention . . . as if her own heart were on the gridiron, and her immortal happiness were involved in its being done precisely ''to a turn!''
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, vii.}}

'''To serve a turn, the turn,''' or '''one’s turn,''' to be sufficient for the purpose, occasion, or emergency; answer the purpose.
{{smaller block|A cloak as long as thine will ''serve the turn.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 131.}}}}
'''To take a turn,''' to take a short walk, ride, or drive. See def. 8.—'''To take one’s turn,''' to occupy the place belonging to one, or to do what is assigned to one, in proper or allotted order.—'''To take turns,''' to take each the other’s place alternately.—'''Turn about.''' See ''about.''—'''Turn and turn about.''' Same as ''turn about.''
{{smaller block|Tacitus says that the land in his time was occupied by the whole community ''turn and turn about.'' {{right|''Brougham.''}}
<poem>Enoch would hold possession for a week:
“This is my house, and this my little wife.”
“Mine too,” said Philip, “''turn and turn about.''”</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}
'''Turn of life.''' See ''menopause.''—'''Turn toll.''' See ''toll''<sup>1</sup>.

'''turnabout''' (tėrn′a-bout″), ''n.'' '''1.''' A merry-go-round; a carrousel.
{{smaller block|The high swings and the ''turnabouts;'' the tests of the strength of limb and lung. ''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXIX. 560.}}
'''2.''' One who turns things about; an agitator; an innovator.
{{smaller block|Our modern ''turnabouts'' cannot evince us but that we feel we are best affected when the great mysteries of Christ are celebrated upon anniversary festivals.
{{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, ii. 36. (''Davies.'')}}}}
'''3.''' A disease in cattle characterized by giddiness and staggering.
{{smaller block|The ''Turn-about'' and Murrain trouble Cattel.
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Furies.}}}}

'''turn-again-gentlemen''' (tėrn′ạ-gen-jen′tl-men), ''n.'' The martagon, or Turk’s-cap lily. ''Britten and Holland.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''Turnagra''' (tėr′nạ-grä), ''n.'' [NL. (Lesson, 1837), prob. < ''Tur''(''dus'') + (''Ta'')''nagra''.] A genus of thrush-like birds peculiar to New Zealand. {{smaller|''T. crassirostris'', originally described by Latham in 1783 as the}}
{{smaller|thick-billed thrush, was formerly common on the South Island of New Zealand, but is now nearly extinct. A second species is ''T. tanagra'' of the North Island. Also called ''Keropia'', ''Otagon'', and ''Ceropia''.}}

[[File:century v08 p0344 c3f1.png|center|165px]]
{{c|{{smaller|''Turnagra crassirostris.''}}}}

'''turnback''' (tėrn′bak), ''n.'' In ''saddlery'', a local name for the strap which goes from the hames back to the hip-strap. See cut under ''harness.''

'''turn-bench''' (tėrn′bench), ''n.'' A simple portable lathe, used by clock- and watch-makers.

'''turn-bridge''' (tėrn′brij), ''n.'' A swing- or swivel-bridge; a pivot-bridge. Also ''turning-bridge. E. H. Knight.'' See cut under ''bridge''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|The span of all the ''turnbridges'' is 75 ft. in the clear.
{{right|''The Engineer'', LXX. 391.}}}}

'''turnbroach†''' (tėrn′brōch), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''turn-broche''; < ''turn'', ''v.'', + obj. ''broach.''] A turnspit.
{{smaller block|''Turne-broches'', les galopins.
{{right|''Palsgrave'', p. 909 (Du Guez, Introductorie).}}
<poem>Has not a deputy married his cook-maid?
An alderman’s widow one that was her ''turn-broach?''</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, iii. 1.}}}}

'''turnbuckle''' (tėrn′buk″l), ''n.'' A device for connecting and tightening two parts of a metal rod or bar. {{smaller|It is essentially a right-and-left screw coupling. A common form is that of a link one or both
ends of which screw on the ends of the parts of the bar; if one end, the other is fitted with a swivel; if both ends, one has a right-handed and the other a left-handed screw.—'''Pipe-turnbuckle''', a right-and-left pipe-coupling.—'''Sin-'''}}
